bull_bear.body:
- Long-standing BOT/PPP concession experience — incorporated in 2006, with a record of developing, operating and maintaining national and state highways across six states (Uttar Pradesh, Kerala, Haryana, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Odisha)
- Board skills matrix explicitly identifies deep domain knowledge of the Roads and Highways sector, including sectoral policy, regulatory affairs and analysis of contractual obligations
- Resilient toll operations at the operational Kerala asset — GIPL maintained uninterrupted toll operations and stable revenue despite judicial interventions and external political factors, with Average Daily Traffic up 2.7% year on year
- Integrated capability set spanning project development, tolling and highway management plus in-house advisory, construction supervision and debt syndication for its own projects
- EPC contracts entered with cost escalation provisions to protect margins, and a working capital cycle the Company describes as highly optimised
bull_bear.title: Bull — competitive strengths

bull_bear.body:
- Growth risk — inability to win new BOT projects at attractive IRRs or acquire existing projects at favourable valuations — Management states growth risk involves the challenge of executing business plans across organic and inorganic avenues and can impair the ability to bid successfully for new projects at attractive Internal Rates of Return or to acquire existing projects at favourable valuations. With the Company currently operating and managing only one highway asset, replenishing the portfolio is existential; mitigation is limited to reviewing market opportunities and bidding selectively against defined investment criteria.
- Regulatory and concession-policy risk — NHAI's new limits on arbitration claims and awards reprice the whole bidding framework — Operations are significantly influenced by government policies. NHAI has introduced limitations on arbitration-related claims and awards in upcoming tenders; while intended to improve fiscal certainty, these alter the risk allocation framework between the Authority and private concessionaires, and management says prospective bidders including the Company must reassess commercial assumptions, pricing strategies and long-term project viability before participating in new tenders. For a company whose value largely rests on pursuing outstanding claims, a regime that caps arbitration recovery is structurally adverse.
- Judicial restriction on toll rate revision at the sole operational asset — Interim orders of the Hon'ble High Court of Kerala continue to restrict implementation of revised toll rates at the GIPL Thrissur-Angamali project, with the revised user fee notification remaining un-implemented. The effect is measurable: LMV traffic rose 2.3% but LMV revenue growth was limited to just 0.76%. Because the Company has one operating asset, a single court order caps the revenue of essentially the whole operating business, and recovery depends on legal and contractual remedies rather than operations.
- Single-asset and single-activity concentration — The Company is currently operating and managing one highway asset, in one state (Kerala), through one subsidiary (GIPL), and its standalone revenue from operations is toll-related income from that subsidiary. Traffic, weather, local political disruption, court orders or a maintenance obligation at that one corridor flow straight through to group performance — the Corporate Overview itself notes judicial interventions and external political factors beyond reasonable control impacting operations and revenue, and suspension of toll collection for a certain period at a subsidiary.
- Subsidiary insolvency and loss of control — CIRP at Solapur Tollways Private Limited — CIRP was initiated against wholly owned subsidiary STPL w.e.f. 20th December 2024 under section 7 of the IBC before the NCLT Kolkata Bench. Pursuant to the NCLT order the Company has ceased to exercise control under Ind-AS 110, impaired the carrying value of its investments and receivables in STPL, and STPL is no longer consolidated — the single largest driver of the year-on-year change in consolidated revenue. The resolution outcome remains outside the Company's control pending a final resolution plan.
- Business risk — capital intensity, funding availability and competitive bidding pressure — Management flags competition, capital intensiveness, input costs and traffic growth for BOT projects as business risks. As the sector grows, more players qualify to bid, heightening competition; the capital-intensive nature of fund-based BOT-toll, HAM and TOT models requires sufficient funds to be available. Stated mitigants are a highly optimised working capital cycle and EPC contracts carrying cost escalation provisions.
- Input cost escalation and supply chain disruption in maintenance obligations — Unexpected input cost increases can directly impact margins. Concretely, sharp escalation in bituminous material prices and supply chain disruptions linked to geopolitical developments in West Asia led GIPL to seek an extension of the overlay schedule from the Authority under MoRTH guidelines while continuing phased maintenance — a contractual obligation (the third cycle of Major Maintenance) whose cost and timing the Company does not fully control.
- Promoter shareholding pledged, and a pending promoter stake transfer — As on March 31, 2026, 22.92% of Promoter and Promoter Group shareholding is under pledge, representing 11.91% of paid-up share capital. Separately, promoter Srei Infrastructure Finance Limited intimated a Framework Agreement dated 11th December 2025 with Srei Equipment Finance Limited and Jemtec Engineering Private Limited for the proposed future sale and transfer of 1,66,30,000 equity shares (19.81% of paid-up equity capital) to Jemtec — a prospective change in the ownership base that the Company itself is not party to.
- Key-personnel churn and attrition — Management states undue attrition could lead to project delays and a loss of competitive edge. The year saw substantial senior churn: the Managing Director stepped down w.e.f. 16th September 2025 (a CEO was appointed the next day and the position of Managing Director ceased to exist), the Senior Vice President - Investments resigned, the Board Chairman died in April 2026, and three Independent Directors ceased office during FY26 — leaving 4 Directors, all Independent, as on the date of the Corporate Governance Report against 6 as at 31st March 2026.

business.body: Incorporated in 2006, BRNL is a BOT company that develops, implements, operates and maintains national and state highway projects in India, holding its projects through SPV subsidiaries and associates. Its business is organised into three lines: project development and implementation; tolling operations and highway management; and advisory / project management services including construction supervision and debt syndication for its own projects. It has been involved in national and state highways across Uttar Pradesh, Kerala, Haryana, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra and Odisha, and is currently operating and managing one highway asset in Kerala, the Thrissur-Angamali road project held through its subsidiary Guruvayoor Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd. (GIPL).

outlook.body: The Annual Report discloses no new capex or expansion project for BRNL — the Company is currently operating and managing one highway asset, the Thrissur-Angamali road project in Kerala held through subsidiary Guruvayoor Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd. (GIPL). The only asset-spend activity described is lifecycle maintenance, not growth capex: during the year the Company maintained a cautious approach towards initiating the third cycle of Major Maintenance of the Thrissur-Angamali road project, citing safeguarding of shareholder interests, financial efficiency and cost optimisation while complying with the Concession Agreement and the Independent Engineer's recommendations. Considering the sharp escalation in bituminous material prices and supply chain disruptions linked to geopolitical developments in West Asia, GIPL sought an extension of the overlay schedule from the Authority in accordance with MoRTH guidelines while continuing phased maintenance activities to ensure public safety and convenience. On the technology side the Company is strengthening its IT systems and has taken steps towards adopting Automatic Number Plate Recognition (ANPR) to strengthen digital toll revenue collection, improve ETC transaction efficiency, reduce manual data entry errors and minimise congestion at toll lanes. No new concession win, bid, award, commissioning timeline or expansion quantum is stated anywhere in this bundle; the sector-level pipeline figures the MD&A cites (the MoRTH 13,400 km / Rs 8.3 Lakh Crore PPP pipeline, NHAI's FY2026-27 monetisation list of 17 assets spanning 1,692.5 km) are GOVERNMENT-wide programme figures, not BRNL projects or commitments.
outlook.title: Capex & expansion plans

outlook.body:
- India's roads and highways sector is positioned as central to infrastructure-led growth, with the National Highway network having expanded around 61% from 91,287 km in FY2013-14 to 1,46,572 km as of March 2026 — management presents sustained public investment in highways as the backdrop for its business.
- Renewed policy focus on private participation through BOT, HAM, TOT and InvIT models: MoRTH has identified a PPP project pipeline of 13,400 km at an estimated cost of Rs 8.3 Lakh Crore to be developed over the next three years, which management frames as the opportunity set for road developers.
- Bharatmala Pariyojana remains central to corridor-based development, envisaging 34,800 km of National Highway corridors at an estimated outlay of Rs 5.35 Lakh Crore.
- Asset monetisation is described as a key opportunity for long-term investors: NHAI realised over Rs 28,300 Crore through InvIT and TOT routes in FY2025-26, and has identified 17 highway assets spanning 1,692.5 km across nine states for monetisation through TOT and InvIT routes in FY2026-27 — allowing private investors to participate in operational road assets with established traffic histories.
- Allied infrastructure — Multimodal Logistics Parks, port connectivity roads, wayside amenities, digital tolling and intelligent transport systems — is widening the scope for private investment beyond highway construction.
- Macro demand backdrop: real GDP grew 7.7% in FY2025-26 with construction activity buoyant on the Government's infrastructure focus, and the RBI projects real GDP growth of 6.6% in FY2026-27 supported by continued public capital expenditure.
- Management flags the downside counterweight: geopolitical tensions, volatility in global energy prices, trade policy uncertainty and supply chain disruptions remain key risks to the pace of growth, with the IMF projecting global growth moderating to 3.1% in 2026.
- Consolidated revenue fell year on year primarily because one subsidiary ceased to be consolidated following its admission into CIRP in FY 2024-25 and the consequent cessation of control, compounded by suspension of toll collection for a certain period at another subsidiary — a structural change in the consolidated revenue base rather than an operating decline.

It has been involved in national and state highways across Uttar Pradesh, Kerala, Haryana, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra and Odisha, and is currently operating and managing one highway asset in Kerala, the Thrissur-Angamali road project held through its subsidiary Guruvayoor Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd. (GIPL).

group_structure.title: Group structure (subsidiaries / JV / related parties)
group_structure.body:
- Solapur Tollways Private Limited (STPL) — subsidiary: Wholly owned subsidiary (100.00% effective shareholding), acquired 3rd August 2013; BOT road SPV. Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process initiated w.e.f. 20th December 2024 under section 7 of the IBC before the NCLT Kolkata Bench; pursuant to the NCLT order dated December 20, 2024 the Company ceased to exercise control over STPL under Ind-AS 110 and no longer consolidates it, while continuing to hold its shares until a final resolution plan. Listed as a related-party subsidiary 'till December 20, 2024'.
- Orissa Steel Expressway Private Limited — subsidiary: Subsidiary, 59.38% effective shareholding, acquired 12th November 2016; road SPV in Odisha. Related-party transactions during the year comprised loans given and investment pledged as collateral for loan taken by the subsidiary. Proposed related-party transaction value for 1st Oct 2026 to 30th Sep 2027 placed before the AGM as a subsidiary counterparty.
- Guruvayoor Infrastructure Private Limited (GIPL) — subsidiary: Subsidiary, 73.99% effective shareholding, acquired 28th March 2018; holds and operates the Company's sole operational highway asset, the Thrissur-Angamali road project in Kerala, and manages its toll operations and major maintenance. Related-party dealings comprise toll revenue income, reimbursement of expenses and unsecured loans given.
- Kurukshetra Expressway Private Limited — associate: Associate, 49.00% extent of holding (5,10,86,910 shares), associated since 28th March 2013; significant influence through control of 49.00% of total share capital; consolidated as an associate and named as an AGM related-party counterparty.
- Mahakaleshwar Tollways Private Limited — associate: Associate, 45.67% extent of holding (4,99,95,000 shares), associated since 28th October 2016; significant influence through control of 45.67% of total share capital; named as an AGM related-party counterparty.
- Srei Venture Capital Trust A/C - Infrastructure Project Development Capital — related party: Investor having significant influence, per the IndAS 24 related-party disclosure
- Srei Infrastructure Finance Limited (SIFL) — related party: Promoter of the Company; party to the Framework Agreement dated 11th December 2025 for the proposed future sale and transfer of 19.81% of the Company's paid-up equity share capital to Jemtec Engineering Private Limited
- Jemtec Engineering Private Limited — related party: Proposed future acquirer of 1,66,30,000 equity shares (19.81% of paid-up equity share capital) under the Framework Agreement dated 11th December 2025 between SIFL, Srei Equipment Finance Limited and Jemtec; the Company is not a party to that agreement

products.title: Products & brands
products.body:
- **Project development and implementation:** BOT road and highway project development
- **Tolling Operations and Highway Management:** Toll collection and highway operations & maintenance, Thrissur-Angamali road project (Kerala, through GIPL)
- **Advisory Services and Project Management Services:** Construction supervision, Debt syndication for the Company's projects

end_markets.title: End Markets (RHP)
end_markets.body:
- India — national and state highway concessions awarded by authorities such as NHAI
- Kerala (the one operational highway asset currently operated and managed)
- States where the Company has developed / operated / maintained highways: Uttar Pradesh, Kerala, Haryana, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Odisha
- Highway users — commercial vehicle (truck/bus) and light motor vehicle toll traffic

demand_drivers.title: Demand & outlook drivers
demand_drivers.body:
- India's roads and highways sector is positioned as central to infrastructure-led growth, with the National Highway network having expanded around 61% from 91,287 km in FY2013-14 to 1,46,572 km as of March 2026 — management presents sustained public investment in highways as the backdrop for its business.
- Renewed policy focus on private participation through BOT, HAM, TOT and InvIT models: MoRTH has identified a PPP project pipeline of 13,400 km at an estimated cost of Rs 8.3 Lakh Crore to be developed over the next three years, which management frames as the opportunity set for road developers.
- Bharatmala Pariyojana remains central to corridor-based development, envisaging 34,800 km of National Highway corridors at an estimated outlay of Rs 5.35 Lakh Crore.
- Asset monetisation is described as a key opportunity for long-term investors: NHAI realised over Rs 28,300 Crore through InvIT and TOT routes in FY2025-26, and has identified 17 highway assets spanning 1,692.5 km across nine states for monetisation through TOT and InvIT routes in FY2026-27 — allowing private investors to participate in operational road assets with established traffic histories.
- Allied infrastructure — Multimodal Logistics Parks, port connectivity roads, wayside amenities, digital tolling and intelligent transport systems — is widening the scope for private investment beyond highway construction.
- Macro demand backdrop: real GDP grew 7.7% in FY2025-26 with construction activity buoyant on the Government's infrastructure focus, and the RBI projects real GDP growth of 6.6% in FY2026-27 supported by continued public capital expenditure.
- Management flags the downside counterweight: geopolitical tensions, volatility in global energy prices, trade policy uncertainty and supply chain disruptions remain key risks to the pace of growth, with the IMF projecting global growth moderating to 3.1% in 2026.
- Consolidated revenue fell year on year primarily because one subsidiary ceased to be consolidated following its admission into CIRP in FY 2024-25 and the consequent cessation of control, compounded by suspension of toll collection for a certain period at another subsidiary — a structural change in the consolidated revenue base rather than an operating decline.

capex_expansion.title: Capex & expansion plans
capex_expansion.body: The Annual Report discloses no new capex or expansion project for BRNL — the Company is currently operating and managing one highway asset, the Thrissur-Angamali road project in Kerala held through subsidiary Guruvayoor Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd. (GIPL). The only asset-spend activity described is lifecycle maintenance, not growth capex: during the year the Company maintained a cautious approach towards initiating the third cycle of Major Maintenance of the Thrissur-Angamali road project, citing safeguarding of shareholder interests, financial efficiency and cost optimisation while complying with the Concession Agreement and the Independent Engineer's recommendations. Considering the sharp escalation in bituminous material prices and supply chain disruptions linked to geopolitical developments in West Asia, GIPL sought an extension of the overlay schedule from the Authority in accordance with MoRTH guidelines while continuing phased maintenance activities to ensure public safety and convenience. On the technology side the Company is strengthening its IT systems and has taken steps towards adopting Automatic Number Plate Recognition (ANPR) to strengthen digital toll revenue collection, improve ETC transaction efficiency, reduce manual data entry errors and minimise congestion at toll lanes. No new concession win, bid, award, commissioning timeline or expansion quantum is stated anywhere in this bundle; the sector-level pipeline figures the MD&A cites (the MoRTH 13,400 km / Rs 8.3 Lakh Crore PPP pipeline, NHAI's FY2026-27 monetisation list of 17 assets spanning 1,692.5 km) are GOVERNMENT-wide programme figures, not BRNL projects or commitments.

moat.title: Bull — competitive strengths
moat.body:
- Long-standing BOT/PPP concession experience — incorporated in 2006, with a record of developing, operating and maintaining national and state highways across six states (Uttar Pradesh, Kerala, Haryana, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Odisha)
- Board skills matrix explicitly identifies deep domain knowledge of the Roads and Highways sector, including sectoral policy, regulatory affairs and analysis of contractual obligations
- Resilient toll operations at the operational Kerala asset — GIPL maintained uninterrupted toll operations and stable revenue despite judicial interventions and external political factors, with Average Daily Traffic up 2.7% year on year
- Integrated capability set spanning project development, tolling and highway management plus in-house advisory, construction supervision and debt syndication for its own projects
- EPC contracts entered with cost escalation provisions to protect margins, and a working capital cycle the Company describes as highly optimised

risks.title: Bear — key risks
risks.body:
- Growth risk — inability to win new BOT projects at attractive IRRs or acquire existing projects at favourable valuations — Management states growth risk involves the challenge of executing business plans across organic and inorganic avenues and can impair the ability to bid successfully for new projects at attractive Internal Rates of Return or to acquire existing projects at favourable valuations. With the Company currently operating and managing only one highway asset, replenishing the portfolio is existential; mitigation is limited to reviewing market opportunities and bidding selectively against defined investment criteria.
- Regulatory and concession-policy risk — NHAI's new limits on arbitration claims and awards reprice the whole bidding framework — Operations are significantly influenced by government policies. NHAI has introduced limitations on arbitration-related claims and awards in upcoming tenders; while intended to improve fiscal certainty, these alter the risk allocation framework between the Authority and private concessionaires, and management says prospective bidders including the Company must reassess commercial assumptions, pricing strategies and long-term project viability before participating in new tenders. For a company whose value largely rests on pursuing outstanding claims, a regime that caps arbitration recovery is structurally adverse.
- Judicial restriction on toll rate revision at the sole operational asset — Interim orders of the Hon'ble High Court of Kerala continue to restrict implementation of revised toll rates at the GIPL Thrissur-Angamali project, with the revised user fee notification remaining un-implemented. The effect is measurable: LMV traffic rose 2.3% but LMV revenue growth was limited to just 0.76%. Because the Company has one operating asset, a single court order caps the revenue of essentially the whole operating business, and recovery depends on legal and contractual remedies rather than operations.
- Single-asset and single-activity concentration — The Company is currently operating and managing one highway asset, in one state (Kerala), through one subsidiary (GIPL), and its standalone revenue from operations is toll-related income from that subsidiary. Traffic, weather, local political disruption, court orders or a maintenance obligation at that one corridor flow straight through to group performance — the Corporate Overview itself notes judicial interventions and external political factors beyond reasonable control impacting operations and revenue, and suspension of toll collection for a certain period at a subsidiary.
- Subsidiary insolvency and loss of control — CIRP at Solapur Tollways Private Limited — CIRP was initiated against wholly owned subsidiary STPL w.e.f. 20th December 2024 under section 7 of the IBC before the NCLT Kolkata Bench. Pursuant to the NCLT order the Company has ceased to exercise control under Ind-AS 110, impaired the carrying value of its investments and receivables in STPL, and STPL is no longer consolidated — the single largest driver of the year-on-year change in consolidated revenue. The resolution outcome remains outside the Company's control pending a final resolution plan.
- Business risk — capital intensity, funding availability and competitive bidding pressure — Management flags competition, capital intensiveness, input costs and traffic growth for BOT projects as business risks. As the sector grows, more players qualify to bid, heightening competition; the capital-intensive nature of fund-based BOT-toll, HAM and TOT models requires sufficient funds to be available. Stated mitigants are a highly optimised working capital cycle and EPC contracts carrying cost escalation provisions.
- Input cost escalation and supply chain disruption in maintenance obligations — Unexpected input cost increases can directly impact margins. Concretely, sharp escalation in bituminous material prices and supply chain disruptions linked to geopolitical developments in West Asia led GIPL to seek an extension of the overlay schedule from the Authority under MoRTH guidelines while continuing phased maintenance — a contractual obligation (the third cycle of Major Maintenance) whose cost and timing the Company does not fully control.
- Promoter shareholding pledged, and a pending promoter stake transfer — As on March 31, 2026, 22.92% of Promoter and Promoter Group shareholding is under pledge, representing 11.91% of paid-up share capital. Separately, promoter Srei Infrastructure Finance Limited intimated a Framework Agreement dated 11th December 2025 with Srei Equipment Finance Limited and Jemtec Engineering Private Limited for the proposed future sale and transfer of 1,66,30,000 equity shares (19.81% of paid-up equity capital) to Jemtec — a prospective change in the ownership base that the Company itself is not party to.
- Key-personnel churn and attrition — Management states undue attrition could lead to project delays and a loss of competitive edge. The year saw substantial senior churn: the Managing Director stepped down w.e.f. 16th September 2025 (a CEO was appointed the next day and the position of Managing Director ceased to exist), the Senior Vice President - Investments resigned, the Board Chairman died in April 2026, and three Independent Directors ceased office during FY26 — leaving 4 Directors, all Independent, as on the date of the Corporate Governance Report against 6 as at 31st March 2026.

hero.oneLiner: Bharat Road Network Limited is a Build-Operate-Transfer (BOT) road developer incorporated in 2006, focused on the development, implementation, operation and maintenance of road and highway projects in India, currently operating and managing one highway asset in Kerala.
